title: Debridement of an open fracture with external fixation
subtitle: Orthoplastic wound excision, lavage and spanning frame

sources.org: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE)
sources.title: Fractures (complex): assessment and management (NG37)

sources.org: FLOW Investigators. N Engl J Med 373:2629
sources.title: A trial of wound irrigation in the initial management of open fracture wounds

sources.org: Gustilo RB, Anderson JT. J Bone Joint Surg Am 58:453
sources.title: Prevention of infection in the treatment of one thousand and twenty-five open fractures of long bones

sources.org: Gustilo RB et al. J Trauma 24:742
sources.title: Problems in the management of type III (severe) open fractures: a new classification of type III open fractures

indications: Every open long-bone, hindfoot or midfoot fracture, within the time standards: immediately when highly contaminated or with vascular compromise, within 12 hours for high-energy fractures and within 24 hours for the rest.
External fixation when definitive internal fixation cannot be followed immediately by definitive soft-tissue cover.
contraindications: None to debridement itself. Physiological instability changes the scale and timing of the operation, not the need for it.
Internal fixation is contraindicated if definitive soft-tissue cover cannot follow at the same sitting.
preparation: Joint orthopaedic and plastic surgery consultant plan for debridement, stabilisation and cover.
Antibiotics already given; wound photographs on the record; neurovascular status documented.
Consent covers further debridement, flap surgery, infection, non-union and the possibility of amputation.
positioning: Supine on a radiolucent table with the limb free and supported.
Tourniquet applied but not routinely inflated.
C-arm access to the whole segment and the joints at either end.
equipment: Debridement set, curettes, rongeurs and bone nibblers.
External fixator set with half-pins, clamps and bars.
A second clean set of instruments, gowns and drapes for after debridement.
anatomy: Perforators from the posterior tibial artery emerge along the medial border of the tibia and supply local fasciocutaneous flaps; incisions must spare them.
The anteromedial surface of the tibia is the safe corridor for half-pins.
Four compartments in the leg, each with its own neurovascular content.
criticalSafety: Debride systematically, layer by layer, from the outside in, to healthy bleeding tissue.
Extend the wound along fasciotomy lines so later flap options are preserved.
Treat everything after debridement as clean surgery: re-prepare, re-drape and use fresh instruments.
Place pins outside the zone of injury and away from where the plastic surgeon will need to work.
structuresAtRisk: Neurovascular bundles at the depth of the wound
Neurovascular structures in the path of half-pins
commonErrors: Debriding to a cosmetic margin rather than a viable one.
Leaving loose cortical fragments without soft-tissue attachment.
Pins placed through the future flap or fixation zone.
Closing a contaminated wound under tension.
complications: Further tissue necrosis requiring repeat debridement.
postop: Return for definitive fixation and soft-tissue cover within 72 hours of injury if not done at this sitting.

steps.emphasis: Limb free on a radiolucent table with the C-arm able to see the joints at both ends of the segment.
Apply but do not inflate unless bleeding obscures the field. Bleeding is how viable tissue identifies itself.
Extend the wound along the fasciotomy lines. The medial incision alone is often enough for debridement and spares the perforators.
Layer by layer: skin, fat, fascia, muscle, then bone. Excise to bleeding, healthy tissue.
Record the Gustilo-Anderson grade now, after debridement, along with the plan and date for definitive cover.

step.oex.bone.title: Bone end debridement
step.oex.bone.why: Devitalised bone is a sequestrum in waiting. Cortical fragments without soft-tissue attachment are dead and will become the focus of infection.
how: Deliver each bone end into the wound by flexing or angulating the limb gently.
Remove loose cortical fragments with no soft-tissue attachment; curette contaminated cancellous bone and the canal ends.
Keep large articular fragments that are needed for joint reconstruction, after cleaning them.
structuresAtRisk: Neurovascular bundle adjacent to the fracture
pitfalls: Keeping a fragment because it fits.
Stripping more periosteum than the injury already has.

step.oex.lavage.title: Low-pressure irrigation
step.oex.lavage.why: Irrigation dilutes what debridement cannot pick out. The FLOW trial supported low-pressure delivery and found more reoperations with soap than with saline.
how: Irrigate with large volumes of saline at low pressure after excision is complete.
Irrigate the canal ends and every recess of the wound.
Do not use irrigation as a substitute for excision.
pitfalls: High-pressure pulsed lavage that drives contamination into tissue planes.

step.oex.reprep.title: Re-preparation and fresh instruments
step.oex.reprep.why: Once debridement is complete, anything implanted or reconstructed at the same sitting should be done as clean surgery, not with the instruments that handled the contamination.
how: Remove the dirty drapes and instruments; the team changes gloves and gowns.
Bring a fresh set of instruments for stabilisation.
pitfalls: Continuing to fixation with the debridement set.

step.oex.frame.title: Spanning external fixator
step.oex.frame.why: A frame holds length and alignment while the soft tissues declare themselves, without placing metal in a contaminated wound.
how: Plan pin sites with the plastic surgeon: outside the zone of injury and away from future flaps and definitive fixation.
Insert two bicortical half-pins in each main fragment through safe corridors, the anteromedial tibia in the leg.
Connect with clamps and bars close to the skin, restore length and alignment under image control, then tighten.
structuresAtRisk: Neurovascular structures in the path of pins
pitfalls: Pins through the wound or the zone of injury.
Bars too far from the bone, producing an unstable frame.
